title: 71 Percent of Indian Americans Disapprove of Trump, but Democrats Are Not Gaining Ground, Carnegie Survey Finds
excerpt: The 2026 Indian American Attitudes Survey reveals a community caught between rising discrimination, weakening partisan loyalty, and a 40 percent emigration consideration rate — all while economic anxiety dominates political priorities.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • 71% of Indian Americans disapprove of Trump's job performance, with strong opposition to his immigration policies.
  • Democratic Party identification has dropped from 52% in 2020 to 46% in 2026, while independents rise to 29%.
  • 40% of Indian Americans have considered leaving the U.S., citing political frustration and cost of living.
  • 31% avoid discussing politics on social media due to fear of discrimination; 19% avoid wearing Indian attire publicly.

  • 71 percent of Indian Americans disapprove of Trump's job performance, with strong opposition to his $100,000 H-1B fee (66 percent oppose) and deportation policies (74 percent oppose)
  • Democratic Party identification has declined from 52 percent in 2020 to 46 percent in 2026, while independents have risen to 29 percent — the highest level recorded
  • Nearly 40 percent of Indian Americans have considered leaving the United States, citing frustration with politics (58 percent), cost of living (54 percent), and personal safety (41 percent)
  • 31 percent of respondents avoid discussing politics on social media for fear of discrimination; 19 percent avoid wearing Indian attire in public

A Community in Political Flux

One year into President Donald Trump's second term, Indian Americans are deeply dissatisfied with his presidency but increasingly skeptical of the Democratic alternative, according to the 2026 Indian American Attitudes Survey released by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

The nationally representative survey of 1,000 Indian American adults, conducted in partnership with YouGov between November 2025 and January 2026, paints a portrait of a community caught between rising discrimination, weakening party loyalties, and persistent economic anxiety — a state the researchers describe as "turbulence."

Seventy-one percent of respondents disapprove of Trump's job performance, with 55 percent expressing strong disapproval. Only 29 percent approve — virtually identical to the assessment Indian Americans made in 2020 at the end of Trump's first term. Indian Americans are substantially more critical of Trump than the general US population, regardless of gender.

"Republican Indian Americans back enforcement-oriented actions but are nearly split on ending birthright citizenship."

"Republican Indian Americans back enforcement-oriented actions but are nearly split on ending birthright citizenship."

Immigration Policy Draws the Sharpest Opposition

Trump's immigration agenda faces overwhelming opposition from Indian Americans. Seventy-four percent oppose the deportation of immigrants to third countries. Two-thirds oppose the $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions — a policy that disproportionately affects the Indian American community, whose members constituted 71 percent of new H-1B petitions in Fiscal Year 2024, according to USCIS data.

"Large majorities of Indian Americans disapprove of Trump's agenda; this disapproval has not produced a commensurate consolidation around the Democratic Party."

— Carnegie Endowment for International Peace

Support for Trump's immigration policies varies sharply by party. Republican Indian Americans back enforcement-oriented actions but are nearly split on ending birthright citizenship. Even among Republican respondents, support weakens when asked about specific policies rather than immigration in the abstract.

Democrats Lose Ground Without Republicans Gaining

Shifting Party Loyalties

Carnegie Endowment for International Peace

The survey's most striking finding is that widespread disapproval of Trump has not translated into gains for Democrats. Democratic identification among Indian Americans has declined steadily from 52 percent in 2020 to 46 percent in 2026. Republican identification has risen modestly from 15 to 19 percent over the same period. The biggest shift has been toward independence — 29 percent of respondents now identify as independents, up six points since 2020.

Ideologically, Indian Americans cluster most heavily at the center. Moderates represent the largest single group at 32 percent, a four-point increase from 2024. The community is best characterized as centrist with a left-of-center tilt, with extremes on either side accounting for no more than 15 percent.

Economic concerns dominate the community's policy priorities. Inflation and prices rank as the most important personal issue (21 percent), followed by jobs and the economy (17 percent). Foreign policy, including US-India relations, barely registers — just 2 percent name it as their top concern.

Discrimination Is Reshaping Daily Life

The survey documents widespread behavioral changes driven by fear of discrimination. Nearly one-third of respondents (31 percent) avoid discussing politics on social media. Twenty-one percent refrain from displaying political signs. Nineteen percent avoid wearing Indian attire in public. Eighteen percent avoid political rallies or protests entirely.

Concerns Driving Emigration Consideration
›58% cite frustration with politics as a reason for considering emigration.
›54% mention cost of living as a concern.
›41% express worries about personal safety.
›62% of those considering leaving do not plan to return to India.
Carnegie Endowment for International Peace

Nearly 40 percent of respondents have thought about leaving the United States altogether. Among those who have considered emigration, frustration with US politics is the top reason (58 percent), followed by cost of living (54 percent) and personal safety (41 percent). Most who contemplate leaving do not envision returning to India — 62 percent named some other country as their potential destination.

Yet the picture is not uniformly bleak. When asked to advise a hypothetical Indian professional considering a US work visa, nearly two-thirds of respondents recommend applying. The survey's authors conclude that perceived opportunities in the United States continue to outweigh discrimination concerns for most respondents, particularly in professional contexts. Indian Americans are unsettled, the researchers found, but not yet in departure mode.
image_caption: More than 5.2 million Indian Americans make up one of the fastest-growing demographic groups in the United States. A Carnegie Endowment survey finds the community is increasingly unsettled by discrimination and political polarization.
